knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 2.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly contrasts named discrete distribution families on a finite or countable support?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Family choice follows the data-generating story, not integer typing alone. Normal-for-counts or interchangeable families are mismatches.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Match generative story to family; discrete ≠ interchangeable.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Normal for counts, ignoring without-replacement structure, or integer implies Poisson.

choices.label: Named discrete families (geometric, binomial, negative binomial, hypergeometric, Poisson, uniform discrete) share discrete support but differ in generative stories: for example Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval under a constant rate; binomial counts successes in fixed independent trials.
All discrete count data should be modelled as Normal because the Normal is the default family for any numeric column.
Hypergeometric and Poisson are interchangeable whenever counts are non-negative integers.
Discrete families apply only after continuous models fail; integer support alone determines Poisson regardless of generating mechanism.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 2.1.1
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. For a single policy, model the number of claims in a fixed year with a constant rare-event rate and independent increments. Which statement is correct?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Poisson matches rare events in fixed time with constant rate. Normal, automatic hypergeometric, or forced binomial n = 1 are mismatches.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Poisson for rare events; refuse Normal/hypergeometric mismatch.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Normal-by-default or wrong discrete family for the story.

choices.label: Poisson fits: counts of rare events in a fixed interval under a constant rate / independent-increments story. Refuse Normal for a non-negative integer count or hypergeometric when there is no without-replacement draw from a finite success/failure population.
Normal(μ, σ²) fits best because the sample mean and variance can always be matched for any count variable.
Hypergeometric is required because every insurance count problem draws without replacement from a finite population of policies.
Binomial is mandatory because there is one policy, so n = 1 trial always defines a binomial count model for annual claims.
